Determine the generation number for each ID

Source: R/findGeneration.R
findGeneration.Rd

This loops through the entire pedigree one generation at a time. It finds the zeroth generation during first loop. The first time through this loop no sire or dam is in parents. This means that the animals without a sire and without a dam are assigned to generation 0 and become the first parental generation. The second time through this loop finds all of the animals that do not have a sire or do not have a dam and at least one parent is in the vector of parents defined the first time through. The ids that were not assigned as parents in the previous loop are given the incremented generation number.

Usage

findGeneration(id, sire, dam, alignMates = FALSE)

Arguments

id

character vector with unique identifier for an individual

sire

character vector with unique identifier for an individual's father (NA if unknown).

dam

character vector with unique identifier for an individual's mother (NA if unknown).

alignMates

TRUE or FALSE, the default. When TRUE, the generations are aligned so that, where it can be done, an offspring's sire and dam are in the same generation (see "Aligned generations").

Value

An integer vector indication the generation numbers for each id, starting at 0 for individuals lacking IDs for both parents. Any id that cannot be placed — e.g. when the pedigree contains a cycle or references a parent ID that is not itself present as an ego ID — is returned as NA and triggers a warning naming the affected ids. With alignMates = TRUE, an individual lacking IDs for both parents may be in a later generation than 0.

Details

Subsequent trips in the loop repeat what was done the second time through until no further animals can be added to the nextGen vector.

This does not work if the pedigree does not have all parent IDs as ego IDs.

Aligned generations

With alignMates = TRUE, animals are moved to later generations so that, where it can be done, the sire and dam of each offspring are in the same generation, as kinship2's kindepth(align = TRUE) does for drawing. A mating is a sire and dam with an offspring that records both. Starting from the generations above:

  1. The matings whose sire and dam are in different generations are visited in the order of their offspring's generation, then of the sire's id and the dam's id, each mating at most once.

  2. At a visit, if the two still differ, the parent in the earlier generation moves to the generation of its nearest later mate, unless it has moved this way before or is related to one of its later mates other than through their own offspring. Its ancestors, and those of their mates who have no parents, move with it by the same number of generations.

  3. The descendants of the animals moved are put one generation after their later parent, and a mating of a descendant moved this way joins the end of the list, if it has not been visited.

  4. Last, every animal with a known parent is put one generation after its later parent.

kinship2's help describes the method in one sentence ("try to make both parents of each child have the same depth"); these steps were measured from its results. On the pedigrees the tests compare, the aligned generations equal kinship2's on both families of its sample.ped, and on most others, and differ on a few animals of larger pedigrees. Unlike kinship2's, they do not depend on the order of the rows, and they place every offspring after each of its known parents. A perfect alignment does not always exist: an animal related to a later mate stays where it is. Animals that cannot be placed stay NA.

Examples

ped <- data.frame(
  id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"),
  sire = c(NA, NA, "A", "A", NA, "D", "D"),
  dam = c(NA, NA, "B", "B", NA, "E", "E"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ped$gen <- findGeneration(ped$id, ped$sire, ped$dam)
## E, with no parents, mates D, of generation 1, and joins it.
ped$aligned <- findGeneration(ped$id, ped$sire, ped$dam, alignMates = TRUE)
ped
#>   id sire  dam gen aligned
#> 1  A <NA> <NA>   0       0
#> 2  B <NA> <NA>   0       0
#> 3  C    A    B   1       1
#> 4  D    A    B   1       1
#> 5  E <NA> <NA>   0       1
#> 6  F    D    E   2       2
#> 7  G    D    E   2       2
